section_summary: This section documents the State Department’s administration of the voluntary “moral embargo” on aircraft, aviation equipment, technical assistance, aluminum scrap, and other materials connected with Japan’s war in China. It includes extensive public, congressional, missionary, and business correspondence both supporting broader restrictions and challenging or seeking clarification of existing policy, together with reports on aviation gasoline, tetraethyl lead, aircraft parts, coal hydrogenation, petroleum products, and Bolivian mineral exports. The papers also show officials monitoring individual transactions while repeatedly explaining that a comprehensive embargo on war materials would require new legislation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on proposed Japanese cracking plants and the aviation-gasoline moral embargo
subfiles.about: Reports discussions with Mr. Halle and Dr. Egloff about whether constructing petroleum cracking plants in Japan would violate the aviation-gasoline moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Halle argued that leaving technical judgments to competing companies produced inconsistency and that Japanese cracking plants could indirectly support the production of aviation gasoline. Green concluded that a renewed industry meeting was probably inadvisable and that only an embargo on petroleum exports would seriously restrict Japan’s aviation-fuel supply.

subfiles.title: Letter promising a report on Japanese and Soviet gasoline facilities
subfiles.about: Promises a technical report on gasoline-production facilities and tetraethyl lead in Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Howard says Standard Oil has gathered information on Japanese and Soviet refineries, synthetic-fuel and blending plants and expects the completed report by week's end.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Standard Oil’s forthcoming gasoline report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Howard’s preparation of a report on gasoline-production facilities in Japan and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Green thanks Howard for assembling the requested technical information. He states that the Department looks forward to receiving the report.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck note transmitting the Standard-Vacuum despatch
subfiles.about: Calls attention to a Tokyo despatch concerning Standard-Vacuum Oil Company’s attitude toward a possible oil embargo.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck recommends the brief despatch for the Secretary’s attention. He says it illuminates Standard-Vacuum’s prospective response to an American embargo.

subfiles.title: Attitude of the Standard-Vacuum Oil Company Toward a Possible Embargo on Oil Shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: George A. Makinson, American Consul General
subfiles.about: Reports that Standard-Vacuum intended to halt oil shipments to Japan from all its properties if the United States imposed an embargo.
subfiles.summary: The company’s local manager said its directors had decided to cooperate fully with the American government, including by stopping shipments from the Netherlands East Indies. He acknowledged the risk of Japanese seizure and the possibility that the United States might not protect the company’s interests there.

subfiles.title: Appeal to Hornbeck for an embargo on war materials and credits to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on American war materials and credits to Japan, supported by six arguments drawn from Greene’s experience in China.
subfiles.summary: Greene argues that American supplies enable Japan to retain coastal positions, threaten Pacific security, damage American trade, and violate the spirit of the Nine-Power Treaty. He also describes Chinese civilian suffering, refugees, and his own treatment of wounded people during the war.

subfiles.title: Appeal to Hamilton for an embargo on war materials and credits to Japan
subfiles.about: Sends Hamilton a parallel appeal for an embargo on American war supplies and credits to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats six arguments that an embargo would shorten Japanese occupation of China, protect Pacific peace, and uphold treaty commitments. Greene grounds the appeal in his years in China and his direct observation of refugees, wounded civilians, and American matériel in Japanese use.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on aluminum-sheet and aluminum-wire scrap for Japan
subfiles.about: Records a ruling that proposed exports of aluminum sheet and wire scrap to Japan fell within the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Tuttle asks whether twenty tons of aluminum scrap, said unsuitable for aircraft, can be exported; Allen says such recoverable aluminum is covered by the policy for Japan and the USSR, and Tuttle will make no commitment.

subfiles.title: Congressional inquiry about public demands for a Japanese embargo
subfiles.about: Asks how to answer hundreds of constituents seeking an embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Boehne reports letters from responsible citizens across party lines about a Japanese embargo and requests confidential guidance on State's position.

subfiles.title: Reply to Boehne on the legal status of an embargo
subfiles.about: Explains that no existing statute authorizes a general embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Department tells Boehne an embargo needs new legislation, enclosing the December statements on the moral embargo; only three arms-export licenses to Japan were issued since December 1936.

subfiles.title: Judge Cooper’s appeal for an embargo on war materials and aviation gasoline
subfiles.about: Advocates an embargo as a peaceful expression of American opposition to Japan’s invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Cooper argues that public sympathy lies with China and that withholding American war matériel would register opposition without bringing the United States into the war. He predicts that a Japanese victory could lead to expansion across Asia, the East Indies, the Philippines, and Hawaii.

subfiles.title: Reply to Judge Cooper concerning embargo authority
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Answers Cooper by explaining the absence of statutory authority for his proposed embargo.
subfiles.summary: Green says that new legislation would be required to establish a general embargo. He encloses official statements on aircraft, aeronautical materials, and aviation-gasoline technology supplied to countries bombing civilian populations.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to American Friends of the Chinese People embargo letter
subfiles.from: American Friends of the Chinese People
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to the original letter requesting an embargo on war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a February 9, 1940 embargo letter from the American Friends of the Chinese People, file 711.942/585.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on W. Reginald Wheeler’s report of western public opinion
subfiles.about: Records Wheeler’s report that Protestant and missionary contacts in the western United States favored withholding materials from Japan.
subfiles.summary: W. Reginald Wheeler reports nearly universal western sentiment for action against supplies aiding Japan's China campaign and Japanese injury to American interests.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Roger Greene’s embargo inquiry
subfiles.about: Records Greene’s inquiry about prospective pressure on Japan under the Pittman Resolution or other embargo bills.
subfiles.summary: Roger Greene asks if action against Japan is likely soon; Hornbeck says there were no new developments on the proposed legislation.

subfiles.title: Fulmer’s transmittal of the Crape Myrtle Garden Club petition
subfiles.about: Forwards a South Carolina garden club’s petition for an immediate halt to war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fulmer calls a Crape Myrtle Garden Club petition important given any renewal of the expired Japan treaty and asks Hull to consider it.

subfiles.title: Crape Myrtle Garden Club petition against shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Rose Wall Dye and members of the Crape Myrtle Garden Club
subfiles.about: Petitions the United States government to stop essential war-material shipments while Japan continues its aggression against China.
subfiles.summary: The petition alleges that Japan is violating treaties, relying heavily on American materials, and attacking civilians and foreign-supported humanitarian property. It requests an end to shipments of scrap iron, arms, equipment, and other essential war materials and is followed by a long membership list.

subfiles.title: Hull’s reply to Fulmer regarding the garden club petition
subfiles.about: Explains the Department’s standard response to requests for a general embargo and returns the enclosed petition.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that current law does not authorize the requested embargo and that new legislation would be required. He supplies statements on aircraft-related exports and aviation-gasoline technology and notes the small number of arms-export licenses issued to Japan.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note on Chungking despatch 467
subfiles.about: Calls attention to the enclosure to Chungking despatch 467 concerning Chinese views on international affairs.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs note directing review of Chungking despatch 467's enclosure, a Chinese organization's views advocating an American embargo.

subfiles.title: Expression of Views of the Lanchow Cultural Union in Regard to International Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits a Lanchow Cultural Union telegram praising American policy and urging an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson explains that the union regards an American embargo as the only effective means of checking international lawlessness and restoring order in the Far East. He adds biographical information about the organization’s contact, Kansu Education Commissioner Cheng Tung-ho, supplied by Major McHugh.

subfiles.title: Lanchow Cultural Union telegram to Ambassador Johnson
subfiles.about: Asks Ambassador Johnson to convey appreciation for American policy and a request for an embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Lanchow Cultural Union telegram to Ambassador Johnson praising the American stand, including ending the commercial treaty, and urging an embargo to restore order in the Far East.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Roger Greene’s correspondence
subfiles.about: Refers Roger Greene’s correspondence to State Department officials for consideration and acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: Watson formally forwards the material from the White House. The slip requests both review and a reply to the correspondent.

subfiles.title: Roger Greene’s cover letter to General Watson
subfiles.about: Encloses Greene’s appeal to the President and asks Watson to present it promptly.
subfiles.summary: Roger Greene thanks General Watson for showing the enclosed letter to the President.

subfiles.title: Roger Greene’s appeal to the President for economic pressure on Japan
subfiles.about: Urges immediate economic pressure on Japan and presidential support for discretionary embargo legislation.
subfiles.summary: Greene argues that Wang Jingwei's impending Nanjing regime makes the moment right for higher duties on Japanese imports and export restrictions, and asks support for Pittman's bill.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Roger Greene
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene’s letter to the President and refers him to earlier Department replies on war-material sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green assures him that the Department is pursuing its policies in ways consistent with American opinion and the objective of keeping the country at peace. He directs Greene to letters dated February 23, March 12, and March 16 for the Department’s position on war materials.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Irving H. Taylor’s protest against the aircraft moral embargo
subfiles.to: Department of State colleagues and superiors
subfiles.about: Records an aircraft-industry demand that the moral embargo on exports to Japan be removed, narrowed, or expanded to all war-useful commodities.
subfiles.summary: Taylor contended that the policy unfairly discriminated against aviation manufacturers, harmed an important market, and would divert business to Italy. Green rejected the factual basis of the protest, warned that a public campaign could backfire, and predicted that the government would not reverse the policy.

subfiles.title: Ralph Felton’s inquiry about aviation gasoline and Japanese imports
subfiles.about: Asks why aviation gasoline exports to Japan have not been morally embargoed and what concerned citizens can do.
subfiles.summary: Ralph Felton, a former Nanjing exchange professor, says Americans expected stronger measures after the treaty ended, including aviation-gasoline limits and duties on Japanese imports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ralph Felton on the scope and legal basis of the moral embargo
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Provides official statements on the moral embargo and explains why a general statutory embargo is not in force.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the President’s statement and press releases on aircraft-related goods and aviation-gasoline technology for countries bombing civilians. He says such advisory action is exceptional and that a comprehensive embargo on war materials to Japan would require new legislation.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary’s query to Berle about embargo propaganda
subfiles.about: Asks whether Berle is familiar with the attached propaganda material.
subfiles.summary: Assistant Secretary's note calling Berle's attention to advocacy material on Japanese aggression, routing the American Committee correspondence and pamphlet that follow.

subfiles.title: American Committee fundraising and action letter
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Solicits money and political activity for a nationwide campaign to end American assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: American Committee circular says the government awaits stronger evidence of support, outlines a $40,000 spring campaign of mailings, press and radio, and urges action before Congress adjourns.

subfiles.title: China Faces Japan—and America
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Uses statistics, news excerpts, and photographs to argue that American exports sustain Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet lists high American shares of Japanese imports of copper, scrap metal, aircraft, petroleum, vehicles, and other strategic materials. It urges readers to distribute the folder and pressure Congress to stop the United States from serving as an arsenal for Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Chase National Bank’s high-octane gasoline inquiry
subfiles.about: Records advice that high-octane gasoline itself was not included in the moral embargo on shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Attorney John Lockwood asked, for Chase National Bank, about high-octane gasoline; Green answered in the negative and supplied press releases on the embargoes.

subfiles.title: Report of March ethyl-fluid shipment to Japan
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports an Associated Ethyl Company shipment of tetraethyl-lead fluid to Japan during March 1940.
subfiles.summary: Goux reports a March shipment to Japan of 100 drums of Ethyl Fluid aboard the Sagoland, 47,300 pounds of tetraethyl lead, and none to the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment and request for continuing Associated Ethyl reports
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the March ethyl-fluid report and asks for continued monthly reporting.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes no shipments to the Soviet Union, assumes none to Japan or the USSR in January and February, and expects monthly reports.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department letter on January aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Transmits a detailed customs breakdown of aircraft and aircraft-parts exports to Japan in January 1940.
subfiles.summary: Barton responds to Yost’s telephone request for detail beyond the Monthly Summary of Foreign Commerce. The letter appears twice in the file and identifies the accompanying statement as enclosure 58508.

subfiles.title: Customs statement on aircraft parts exported to Japan
subfiles.about: Itemizes January shipments of aircraft engine parts, bearings, pumps, starters, wheels, and accessories to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The statement lists shipments under commodity numbers 7947 and 7949.9, including several large New York consignments and smaller Los Angeles shipments. It notes classification uncertainties, identifies one shipment under State Department license 3921, and says the declarations did not indicate partial shipments for complete aircraft assembly.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum interpreting January aircraft shipments
subfiles.about: Explains why January aeronautical exports valued at $200,000 did not necessarily show a collapse of the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Yost says all listed January aircraft materials were covered by the moral embargo, only the wheels needing a license; the total may be small orders via unregistered supply houses, and Douglas stopped shipping when questioned.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting warnings to major aircraft-parts exporters
subfiles.about: Records a request that Commerce warn the firms responsible for the three largest January aeronautical shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: After reviewing the $200,000 January total, Yost asked Bureau director James Young to remind the exporters behind shipments valued at $74,150, $41,987, and $29,299 of the moral embargo. Young promised to act immediately and report the results; three file copies of the memorandum are present.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about tourmaline discs for Japanese aviation radios
subfiles.about: Requests a ruling on a Japanese requisition for piezo-electric tourmaline discs used in aviation radio transmitters.
subfiles.summary: Nippon Electric sought 100 tourmaline discs worth about $500 from International Standard Electric; Keller notes they aren't on control lists but asks guidance given aviation use.

subfiles.title: Ruling on tourmaline discs for aviation radio transmitters
subfiles.about: Advises that discs intended for aviation radio transmitters fall within the moral embargo on aeronautical equipment.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the December 1939 guidance and states that the proposed discs would be treated as aeronautical equipment. He also warns that possible military secrets should be disclosed to the Department for review before any export sale.

subfiles.title: Request for the Fourth Annual Report of the National Munitions Control Board
subfiles.to: Department of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Thanks the Department for research materials and asks for the National Munitions Control Board’s fourth annual report.
subfiles.summary: Chen, who found seventeen earlier enclosures useful for research on arms-export controls, requests the new Fourth Annual Report of the National Munitions Control Board.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the National Munitions Control Board report
subfiles.about: Sends Chen a copy of the Fourth Annual Report of the National Munitions Control Board.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Chen’s April 4 request. He states that one copy of the report is being transmitted under separate cover.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department referral of Charles Brown’s letter
subfiles.about: Refers Charles O. Brown’s coal-hydrogenation letter to the State Department for attention.
subfiles.summary: Commerce's Young forwards a New York chemical engineer's letter from Charles Brown, who has been told of the referral.

subfiles.title: Warning about Sumitomo coal-hydrogenation equipment
subfiles.to: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Argues that proposed American equipment for Sumitomo’s coal-hydrogenation program should fall under the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Brown warns that Sumitomo coal-hydrogenation equipment would indirectly support Japanese aviation and compares it to restricted aviation-gasoline technology.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to the Secretary of Commerce
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Commerce’s referral of Brown’s letter and encloses the State Department’s response.
subfiles.summary: State acknowledges Commerce's April 5 referral on Charles Brown and sends a copy of its reply for Secretary Hopkins.

subfiles.title: Reply to Charles Brown concerning coal-hydrogenation equipment
subfiles.from: Department of State, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Brown’s warning about bids for Sumitomo coal-hydrogenation equipment.
subfiles.summary: Department summarizes Brown's argument that coal-hydrogenation plants should fall under aviation-gasoline restrictions, says it is under careful consideration, and thanks him.

subfiles.title: Judge Cooper’s clarification advocating embargo legislation
subfiles.about: Clarifies that his earlier letter advocated new embargo legislation rather than assuming that statutory authority already existed.
subfiles.summary: Judge Cooper says he knew no statute authorized a munitions embargo on Japan and argues any embargo should go beyond airplanes and aircraft equipment.

subfiles.title: Japanese diplomatic activity and Bolivian mineral shipments
subfiles.from: Douglas Jenkins, American Legation at La Paz
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchases of Bolivian minerals, possible onward shipments to Germany, and Japanese diplomatic activity in Bolivia.
subfiles.summary: Despatch: February shipments to Japan of 140 tons of wolfram and 500 tons of tin concentrates, claims wolfram and American molybdenum went to Germany by Trans-Siberian rail, and Japanese tin-smelting uncertainty.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting Tokyo’s report on Bolivian ore shipments
subfiles.about: Forwards the La Paz despatch confidentially and requests information about Bolivian ore shipments and smelting capacity in Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Instruction asks Tokyo to investigate reports on Bolivian ore trade, especially Japanese and Manchukuo smelting and ore handling.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on termination of the Japanese-American Commercial Treaty
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to a memorandum narrating the events leading to American notice terminating the 1911 commercial treaty with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to an April 9, 1940 State memorandum on termination of the Japanese-American Commercial Treaty, file 711.942/627.

subfiles.title: Phillips Petroleum report of March shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: K. S. Adams, Phillips Petroleum Company
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Reports March deliveries of commercial iso-octane and naturally occurring petroleum products for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Phillips Petroleum reports March deliveries to Mitsui of 12,700 drums of iso-octane and 2,322 drums of other petroleum products.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Phillips Petroleum’s blending-agent report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Phillips Petroleum’s report on blending agents sold and delivered for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Adams for the April 4 report of blending agents exported during March 1940.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about resuming scrap-rubber exports to Japan and Dairen
subfiles.about: Asks whether the firm may resume buying American scrap rubber for Japanese principals and shipment chiefly to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Brokers inactive three years in scrap-rubber exports to Japan and Dairen ask whether scrap rubber, unlike crude rubber, faces any objection.
